title: Hydrostatic-pressure engineered ZnX (X = O, S) photosensitive gates for junctionless UV phototransistors: a comparative DFT and device-level analysis
content: Hydrostatic-pressure engineering provides a computational route for assessing how lattice expansion and compression modify the electronic structure and ultraviolet (UV) response of wide-bandgap photosensitive materials without changing their chemical composition. In this work, ZnX (X = O, S) semiconductors are comparatively investigated as strain-engineered photosensitive gate layers for junctionless UV phototransistors by combining CASTEP-based density functional theory (DFT) calculations with device-level simulations. Hydrostatic pressure was varied from −7 to +7 GPa, where negative values represent computationally expanded lattice states and positive values represent compressed states. The ZnO bandgap increases from 3.348 to 3.500 eV, corresponding to a modulation of 0.152 eV and a cutoff-wavelength shift from about 370.4 to 354.3 nm. In contrast, ZnS exhibits a much stronger bandgap variation from 3.287 to 4.072 eV, yielding a 0.785 eV modulation and shifting the cutoff wavelength from approximately 377.2 to 304.5 nm. Device simulations using identical n+-Si junctionless channels show that these material-level changes directly modulate the output, transfer, responsivity, photo-to-dark current ratio, and detectivity characteristics through the photogating mechanism. The expanded −7 GPa condition provides the strongest simulated photoresponse, while compression progressively reduces the optoelectronic FoMs. The results identify ZnO as the more strain-stable photosensitive gate and ZnS as the more strongly strain-tunable alternative, demonstrating the potential of ZnX (X = O, S)-gated junctionless phototransistors for strain engineering UV sensing.
